prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the claims-triage agent (home and motor claims assessment within delegated authority) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: cracks appearing in the walls. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 0)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When cracks are hairline and follow plaster joints or recent decoration lines, I treat them as more likely to be cosmetic shrinkage than structural movement, so I look for any accompanying doors sticking, sloping floors or widening over time before escalating."},{"type":"fact","content":"When cracks are wider at one end, run diagonally from openings, or step through brickwork, I flag them as potentially structural and check whether they are progressive rather than new-only-after-weather events."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the claim mentions recent cold snaps, heating being off, or a newly dried-out property, I consider thermal movement and drying shrinkage as a common explanation, especially if there is no matching evidence of impact or settlement."},{"type":"fact","content":"When cracks appear alongside an escape of water, I look for saturation, soft plaster, swelling timber and delayed settlement, because water-related movement can show up as cracking after the leak itself has been contained."},{"type":"preference","content":"When I see repeated reports of the same crack in different rooms, I prefer to ask for a simple sequence of when each one first appeared, because timing often separates one ongoing cause from several unrelated cosmetic defects."},{"type":"observation","content":"When cracks are concentrated around windows, doors or ceilings on upper floors, I treat deflection, seasonal movement and poor previous repairs as common working explanations before assuming wider damage."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the property is older and has been altered, I check whether the cracks line up with extensions, removed walls or patch repairs, because junctions between different materials often move more than original fabric."},{"type":"observation","content":"When there has been storm exposure, I do not assume the crack itself is storm damage unless there is evidence of wind-driven impact, displaced masonry or a clear sudden onset linked to the event."},{"type":"preference","content":"When photos are available, I prefer images that show the crack in context, the approximate width with a ruler or coin, and the full wall or façade, because isolated close-ups are poor at showing whether the pattern is benign or concerning."},{"type":"fact","content":"When a crack is reported without any change in alignment, no fresh moisture and no worsening over time, I lean towards monitoring and signposting rather than immediate repair authority, because stable cracks are often low-risk."}]}
